description:
We are a team of six engineering students: five studying Computer Systems and one studying Mechatronics. This combination lets us cover both the software and hardware sides of a project, from data processing and application development to sensors, electronics, and prototyping.

We are motivated, collaborative, and eager to learn.
summary:
Next Frontier - Mission Design Game 

Next Frontier is a 3D mission design game in which the player runs a small launch company and has to make every number on the vehicle agree with the sky. Take a contract, size the payload, hire a crew whose files meet NASA's published astronaut candidate standard, build a multi-stage rocket, and fly it.

Nothing is scripted. Delta-v comes from the rocket equation, stage by stage. Tank wall thickness comes from hoop stress. The launch is integrated second by second through a U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 with Mach-dependent drag, a gravity turn, staging, and an acceleration limit set by the weakest medical certification aboard. The pad is part of the design: latitude and range azimuth limits decide which orbital plane is reachable at all, and a plane you cannot fly is a bill of thousands of metres per second. The orbit you choose has weather in it, because the debris environment you pick decides your shielding mass and your disposal obligations.

It runs in a browser, so it fits a school laptop. It teaches why propellant, structure, payload and margin are one argument, and it makes orbital mechanics legible to students who would never otherwise meet it.
details:
Next Frontier is a 3D rocket and mission design game. The player runs a small launch company: take a contract, design the payload, recruit a crew, build a vehicle stage by stage, and fly it. Six screens carry the loop: contracts and destination facts, payload design, crew files, the vehicle builder with its flight computer, the 3D flight with map mode, and a flight log that keeps the reason each mission ended the way it did. A guided tour of five cards walks a first-time player from the contract to a flown mission, and a free "creative room" lets a player experiment with the physics and the roster rules without a bank balance in the way.

Every outcome is computed, not animated. Delta-v per stage is the rocket equation. Tank mass comes from its volume, the propellant density and a wall sized by hoop stress with a minimum gauge. The ascent is integrated every second through a U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 with Mach-dependent drag, gravity-turn guidance with a closed loop that aims for a 200 km orbit, staging that has to clear the engine below, and structural break-up when the angle of attack at high dynamic pressure overloads the airframe. A crewed vehicle's peak acceleration is capped by the certification of the weakest seat aboard. The launch site is part of the design: latitude and range azimuth limits decide which planes are reachable, the eastward speed of the ground is credited, and the plane you did not reach is charged as a real plane change. Insertion altitude is priced as a Hohmann climb from the parking orbit. The orbit you choose carries the published debris environment: object flux by altitude and inclination, the aluminium thickness that stops a given particle size, the 25-year disposal rule, and the fragments a break-up leaves behind.

The intended impact is STEM fluency. Players leave with an intuition normally reserved for a mission design course: that propellant, structure, payload and margin are one argument; that a launch site and an orbital plane are engineering constraints rather than map coordinates; and that the debris environment is a design input, not a footnote. Because the game is a browser build with no installation, it reaches a classroom laptop or a school lab, and the tour turns the first mission into a ten-minute lesson that ends in orbit or in an explanation of why not.

Godot 4.7.2 with GDScript and the Compatibility (OpenGL) renderer, plus custom GLSL shaders for the atmosphere, the planet, the exhaust plume, the pad smoke and the hull finishes. The planet is not a mesh: it is ray-traced in a shader with Rayleigh and Mie scattering, a cloud shell, night-side city lights and a Moon, which is what keeps the download small enough for a browser build. Exported to HTML5, Windows, macOS, Linux and Android. Version control in git; a headless test suite and screenshot probes in the repository check the physics models, the interface layout at several window sizes, and a full scripted playthrough. No special hardware is required: it targets integrated graphics with a keyboard and mouse.

The decision we are proudest of is that a seat is not a slot but a file. Crew candidates carry education, test-pilot school, hours in command, height, vision, blood pressure and flight history, and the game reads that file against NASA's published candidate standard and prints exactly which row disqualifies the applicant. The second is that the instruments, the orbit map and the transfer ellipse on the mission screen are drawn from the same numbers the planner bills, so the picture cannot flatter the player. What we weighed: accuracy against playability, with every simplification documented in the repository; readability at 1280x720 and on stretched windows; frame rate on integrated graphics; and honesty, since the game shows its own arithmetic on request instead of hiding it behind a score.
